Quiero que vengas: desejar que outra pes: Quiero que vengas: wanting someone else to do something
PASSO 1: veja primeiro quando usar. Se v: STEP 1: first, when to use it. If you want ANOTHER person to do something, the sentence has two subjects. English links them with an object + infinitive: "I want YOU TO COME". Spanish can't do that: it links the two with «que» and puts the second verb in the subjunctive: «Quiero que vengas» (literally "I want that you come"). STEP 2: when the subject is the SAME, there's no «que» and the second verb stays in the infinitive, as in English: «Quiero venir» (I want to come). STEP 3: verbs of wishing, asking, advising and influence that work this way: querer, desear, esperar, preferir, necesitar, pedir, aconsejar, recomendar, sugerir, exigir, permitir, prohibir, mandar, dejar. English "I need you to…", "I'd prefer you to…", "I'm asking you to…" all become «que» + subjunctive. STEP 4: «ojalá (que)» + subjunctive expresses a wish: «Ojalá llueva» (I hope it rains / let's hope it rains). STEP 5: with «aconsejar, permitir, prohibir, recomendar, dejar, pedir», when there's an indirect object, Spanish also accepts the infinitive, close to English: «Te aconsejo descansar» or «Te aconsejo que descanses» (I advise you to rest). Both are correct. STEP 6: «esperar que» means "to hope that", and here English uses the plain present, which tempts you into the indicative: "I hope you COME" = «Espero que VENGAS», never «espero que vienes». STEP 7: for the forms, use what you learned in lesson 42. STEP 8: in Latin America, «ustedes» replaces «vosotros»: «Quiero que vengan»; some regions also have their own «vos» forms.

Certeza e dúvida: indicativo ou subjunti: Certainty and doubt: indicative or subjunctive?
PASSO 1: a regra é simples. Se você afir: STEP 1: the rule is simple. If you state something as certain, use the indicative. If you doubt it, deny it or present it as merely possible, use the subjunctive. STEP 2: «creer que» and «pensar que» in the affirmative state something: «Creo que viene» (I think he's coming). In the negative they doubt it: «No creo que venga» (I don't think he's coming). English uses the same verb form in both sentences; Spanish switches mood. STEP 3: the same goes for «parecer»: «Me parece que es difícil» and «No me parece que sea difícil». STEP 4: «dudar que» always takes the subjunctive: «Dudo que llegue a tiempo» (I doubt he'll arrive on time). But «no dudar que» affirms, so it takes the indicative: «No dudo que vendrá». STEP 5: expressions of certainty take the indicative: «es verdad que, es cierto que, es evidente que, está claro que, estoy seguro de que». With «no», they take the subjunctive: «No es verdad que sea tarde». STEP 6: expressions of possibility take the subjunctive: «es posible que, es probable que, puede que»: «Es posible que llueva» (It may rain — English "may" is a clue). STEP 7: «quizá, quizás» and «tal vez» (maybe, perhaps) take the subjunctive when you're more doubtful and can take the indicative when you're fairly sure. At B1, use the subjunctive: «Quizá tenga razón». STEP 8: «a lo mejor» (seen before) takes the indicative: «A lo mejor tiene razón». STEP 9: a question like «¿Crees que viene?» usually stays in the indicative, because you're asking, not denying.

Sentimentos e opiniões pedem subjuntivo: Feelings and opinions take the subjunctive
PASSO 1: quando você reage a algo, sente: STEP 1: when you react to something — joy, sadness, surprise, annoyance — or give a judgement, the next verb goes in the subjunctive, even if the fact is true: «Me alegra que estés aquí» (I'm glad you're here — you ARE here, and I'm glad about it). English uses the indicative ("you're here"); Spanish uses the subjunctive because the main point is your reaction. STEP 2: expressions of emotion: «me alegra que, me gusta que, me encanta que, me molesta que, me sorprende que, me da pena que, me da rabia que, siento que, tengo miedo de que». STEP 3: impersonal judgements: «es bueno, es malo, es importante, es necesario, es normal, es raro, es mejor, es increíble, es una pena» + «que» + subjunctive: «Es importante que descanses» (It's important that you rest / for you to rest). STEP 4: if the subject is the same, use the infinitive: «Me alegra verte» or «Me alegro de verte» (I'm glad to see you). If the subjects change, use «que» + subjunctive: «Me alegro de que vengas» (I'm glad you're coming). STEP 5: careful with «siento que». Meaning "I'm sorry that", it takes the subjunctive («Siento que no puedas venir»). Meaning "I feel / sense that", it takes the indicative («Siento que estás cansado»). STEP 6: remember the contrast with certainty: «es verdad que» and «es evidente que» take the indicative, while «es raro que» and «es una pena que» take the subjunctive. STEP 7: in Latin America, say «Me alegra que vengan» instead of «que vengáis».
